entries.title: Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage
entries.summary: Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.
entries.content:
Germany

Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage

August 24, 2026

Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.

The list of international composers who have written for star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter is a long one. It features names like Krzysztof Penderecki and Sofia Gubaidulina, along with Andre Previn and Jörg Widmann. In recent years, women like Iranian-Dutch composer Aftab Darvishi and South Korean composer Unsuk Chin have also written works for Mutter.

On the occasion of the violinist's 50th stage anniversary, she's now recorded over 30 works either dedicated to her or commissioned by her — all part of her "ASM Forte Forward" project on the Alpha Classics label.

The first album in the series, "East Meets West," reflects not just the artist's musical passions but also her social engagement. The opening "Likoo for Solo Violin," composed by Aftab Darvishi for Mutter in 2024, leaves a powerful impression. "Likoo" is a lament about loss, written at a time when especially women in Iran were fighting repression by the regime.

Giving women a voice

"I wanted to create a musical tribute to the people in Iran and to those fighting for freedom, coexistence, empathy and equality, in the hope that these atrocities would never be repeated," Mutter told DW. "War is raging on our wonderful planet even as I'm playing, but I won't give up hope for love and empathy." Mutter's performance of it is deeply moving — one can almost hear the women's cries in the violin, fading into silence.

With the situation in Iran deteriorating, Mutter says it's especially important to her to keep "Likoo" in her repertoire. "I have great admiration for Persian culture and for the female composers who still live in Iran — such as Golfam Khayam, who managed to send me her score by email during a pause in the shelling. I still hear from her from time to time," Mutter says.

"These female composers in Iran fascinate me, and the piece 'Likoo' in particular. That's why — also sadly because of the current situation — it's very important to me to perform 'Likoo' at the anniversary concert." The concert is being held on August 25 at the Lucerne Festival.

Her 1976 stage debut in Lucerne

On August 23, 1976, a 13-year-old Anne-Sophie Mutter took the stage at a young artists' concert in Lucerne. It was there that conductor Herbert von Karajan first encountered the young talent. A year later, he hired her for a concert with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Salzburg Easter Festival. So began Mutter's long collaboration with Karajan and his Berlin orchestra.

Another figure who shaped her musical life on stage in the 1980s was Swiss conductor and patron Paul Sacher. "He was a major influence on my interest in contemporary music," Mutter says. She cherishes the undogmatic learning experience she gained from Sacher and her other mentors. Sacher always afforded her the freedom to decide how she would approach an assignment. He passed a motto on to her: "What I can't do, I can learn. What I can't learn today, I can learn later."

The Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation

A four-time Grammy winner and recipient of Japan's Praemium Imperiale, she's now supporting highly gifted young musicians through the Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation. She encourages her scholarship recipients to embrace social engagement alongside contemporary music. She's herself a supporter of humanitarian organizations such as Save the Children and Doctors Without Borders, and from 2021 to 2025 served as German Cancer Aid's chairwoman.

It's difficult for young musicians to build an audience and make money with contemporary music, Mutter says. "All the same, I want to keep them grounded and show them it's not just about getting rich and famous; they have a role to play in society — in social environments. Playing at a nursing home, for example, or teaching, supporting charitable organizations with benefit concerts."

A platform for composers

As well, Mutter uses the work she commissions — including from former and current scholarship recipients — to help advance their careers. "I want to give these pieces a platform, along with a recorded presence. Without that, these wonderful works couldn't be heard all over the world."

The next album in the "ASM Forte Forward" series being released for the anniversary is "American Tunes #1." It includes works by Andre Previn, whom Mutter was married to for four years, as well as US composer Sebastian Currier, who has written several pieces for Mutter.

"It gives me particular pleasure that many works by colleagues from my foundation, as well as by former and current scholarship recipients, have actually been recorded," Mutter says. "I have managed to put many of my young musicians at the center of this new 'Forte Forward' series, and that makes me very happy."

Albums of memories

To further mark her onstage milestone, Mutter has planned several projects with her longtime label, Deutsche Grammophon. Among them is the release of seven location-centered albums featuring selected works — pieces that, as in the case of the city of Lucerne, were premiered there or hold special significance in Mutter's musical life.

So far, "My Berlin," "My London" and, in connection with the anniversary concert in Lucerne, "My Lucerne" have been released digitally. The seven planned albums will follow the artist around the globe, from Berlin, London and Lucerne to Tokyo and New York.

Anne-Sophie Mutter's constant companion is her Stradivarius violin. "The violin is the coolest instrument in the universe. For 50 years I've tried again and again to show that," she says.

The instrument is her voice, too, she adds: "I find it fascinating how music becomes so expressive precisely where language ends, and how in this cosmos of creativity we can connect, discover ourselves, give ourselves over to expression, and truly experience life."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: US to unveil new Iran sanctions, says war entering 'endgame'
entries.summary: In what Donald Trump has called "economic D-Day," the US says the new economic sanctions will be "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled." Tehran says any support of the measures is an "act of war."
entries.content:
Iran

US to unveil new Iran sanctions, says war entering 'endgame'

August 24, 2026

In what Donald Trump has called "economic D-Day," the US says the new economic sanctions will be "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled." Tehran says any support of the measures is an "act of war."

The US is preparing to unveil a raft of new economic measures targeting Iran and its trade partners amid the stalled six-month old war in the Middle East.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce the measures in a press conference at 1800 GMT on Monday.

Iran, a country that has already been living under international sanctions for decades, has vowed to retaliate.

In a post on X, Bessent described the sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."

He said US President Donald Trump had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities," destroyed nearly 100% of its military factories and "buried its nuclear program."

"We are now entering the endgame," he added.

‘Economic D-Day'

Last week, Trump announced what he called an "economic D-Day" for Tehran, threatening harsher sanctions targeting not only Iran but also countries that continue to do business with it.

"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said.

Already last week, the United Arab Emirates, one of Iran's largest trading partners and its biggest source of imports, announced that it was suspending all trade with Iran.

It was not clear if the US measures will include action against China, Russia and India.

Ahead of Monday's press conference, China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing was monitoring developments closely and would do what is necessary to protect its rights. The ministry also added that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve problems.

How has Iran responded to the new sanctions?

Over the weekend, the head of Iran's top security body warned that Tehran would see any country's support of the US measures as an "act of war."

Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei said Iran would "retaliate in a seismic manner" to the sanctions by targeting other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf.

"If the economic war ​continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said.

The current situation in the Iran war

The Middle East war began on February 28 when Israel and the US carried out strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Tehran responded with strikes on energy infrastructure and US bases in the Gulf region.

While the two sides have stopped the bombing, talks to end the conflict have stalled, with control over the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key sticking point. Iran has effectively closed the waterway, crucial for global oil and gas shipments, while the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports.

Under a memorandum of understanding signed in June, the two sides had 60 days to negotiate an end to the war and reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear program. But that period expired last week with no signs of a deal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief was expected to travel to Iran on Monday as part of efforts to revive diplomatic talks in the conflict.

And on Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister is set meet his Iranian counterpart to continue talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Syria sentences Assad-era top Muslim cleric to life in prison
entries.summary: Muslim cleric Ahmad Hassoun was convicted of crimes including inciting sectarian violence and justifying murder. He is the latest Syrian official aligned with ousted President Bashar Assad to face trial.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

Muslim cleric Ahmad Hassoun was convicted of crimes including inciting sectarian violence and justifying murder. He is the latest Syrian official aligned with ousted President Bashar Assad to face trial.

A Syrian court on Monday handed a life sentence to Ahmad Hassoun, the country's former grand mufti under ex-President Bashar Assad.

The religious cleric, who vocally supported the regime's policies, was found guilty of a raft of crimes including inciting sectarian unrest and justifying murder.

Judge Fakhreddine al-Aryan said the official religious establishment under Assad had "justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law."

A string of trials over civil war

Hassoun is the 10th Assad-era figure to be sentenced under Syria's new authorities.

Earlier this month, Assad himself and his brother Maher were sentenced to death in absentia for atrocities committed during Syria's civil war.

More than half a million people were killed and millions were displaced during the war, which began in 2011 following a crackdown on anti-government protesters. It ended in December 2024 with Assad's ouster in an offensive by Islamist-led militants.

The former president fled Syria as his regime fell and is believed to be in Russia.

Rights groups raise concerns

Death sentences have also been handed to Bashar's cousins, Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, who were tried in person.

The sentences have been welcomed by Syrians who had previously criticized the new government for not moving fast enough to act against Assad-era officials. But human rights groups have voiced concerns that the trials are being rushed and may not be fair.

"Advancing justice for the litany of serious crimes committed in Syria requires more than just convictions, but building a system that can deliver competent, impartial, and independent justice," said Balkees Jarrah, the Middle East and North Africa director for Human Rights Watch.

Who is Ahmad Hassoun?

Hassoun, 77, held the position of Syria's top Islamic cleric from 2005 until 2021, when the position was abolished.

An Aleppo native, he was known for his close ties to Assad and was often seen at his side on religious occasions.

He was arrested at Damascus Airport in March last year while trying to flee the country.

entries.title: Dutch pull out of 'no longer neutral' Eurovision
entries.summary: The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.

Dutch state broadcaster Avrotros said on Monday that the Netherlands will not be taking part in next year's Eurovision Song Contest (ESC).

The event can "no longer be considered neutral," given the war in Gaza, it said.

Eurovision boycotts

This year, the Netherlands was joined by Spain, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia in staging the biggest political boycott in Eurovision history in protest at Israel's participation. Hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters also marched outside the event. 

Avrotros Director-General Taco Zimmerman said international conflicts were increasingly affecting the contest and "undermining its neutral character," adding that it had "become a platform for division."

Earlier this month, ESC organizers announced new rules that bar any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced ‌changes ... do not provide sufficient confidence that ​the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest ⁠has ​been restored," Avrotros ​said.

The pop spectacle is watched by tens of millions of viewers around the world each year.

Israel came close to winning the competition in 2025 and 2026, placing second in both events.

The 2027 ESC will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, after singer Dara won this year's competition in Vienna, Austria.

The Netherlands and Eurovision: 'Very close to our hearts'

The Netherlands took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.

They have won it five times since then, most recently in 2019 with Duncan Laurence and his song "Arcade."

According to the Eurovision website, it was the first competition entry to reach 1 billion streams on Spotify.

The country's withdrawal from the next Eurovision is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," Zimmerman said.

"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Scientists discover new 'immune hubs' in skull bone marrow
entries.summary: In mouse skull marrow, 'immune hubs' that actively defend the brain have been discovered. Similar cells exist in human skulls, but their role remains unclear.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

In mouse skull marrow, 'immune hubs' that actively defend the brain have been discovered. Similar cells exist in human skulls, but their role remains unclear.

The skull has traditionally been regarded largely as armor for the brain. New research from the United States suggests it may have another role: proactively helping to defend what lies beneath it.

Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis identified previously unknown immune "security stations" in the bone marrow of mouse skulls.

What the mouse experiments revealed

The lymph node-like structures responded to brain tumors before more distant lymph nodes in the neck did. When researchers disrupted the structures in mice with glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, the tumors grew faster and the animals died sooner.

"The skull should no longer be viewed simply as a protective shell around the brain," senior study author Jonathan Kipnis told DW.

"It contains specialized immune environments that appear capable of responding locally to changes within the brain."

The discovery, published in the journal "Nature," comes with an important caveat: The researchers have so far only demonstrated how the structures function in mice, not humans.

Kipnis cautioned that the human evidence remains preliminary: "We found similar immune cells in human skull marrow, suggesting that related structures may exist, but we have not yet demonstrated that they are organized or function in the same way as those in mice," he said.

How scientists' view of brain immunity changed

For much of the 20th century, the brain was described as "immune privileged" — unusually protected from immune activity because inflammation that is useful elsewhere can damage delicate brain tissue.

The blood-brain barrier, which tightly controls what can pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue, reinforced the idea that the brain was largely isolated from the body's conventional immune system.

That picture has changed dramatically.

Researchers now know that the brain communicates continuously with the immune system, particularly through tissues surrounding the brain.

Kipnis' lab helped drive that rethink in previous work, first by identifying lymphatic vessels in the membranes surrounding the brain and later by showing tiny channels connecting those membranes to the skull's bone marrow.

"The traditional concept of immune privilege has already changed substantially," Kipnis said. "Our findings add another layer by showing that specialized immune structures exist within the skull bone marrow, immediately adjacent to the brain."

How the skull's immune hubs are organized

The researchers tracked proteins moving from mouse brains through microscopic skull channels and into the bone marrow.

There they found organized clusters of so-called B cells and T-cells. T cells help B cells in "creating large amounts of powerful antibodies that help fight disease and infection."

Finding immune cells in bone marrow was not unusual. The surprise was their organization into structures resembling lymph nodes elsewhere in the body. These immune hubs are where immune cells work together to respond to threats.

Being so close to the brain could allow the immune hubs a faster, more specialized immune response.

"The lymph nodes in the neck are 'shared' with tissues such as the mouth, throat and skin," Kipnis said.

"The skull structures may provide the brain with something resembling its own dedicated lymph nodes, allowing immune responses to be coordinated locally."

Why the skull immune hubs are significant

"We have never seen such structures in healthy bone marrow before," study co-author Jang Hyun Park said. "It is an exciting discovery that points out that a complex brain requires its own specialized immune structures to defend it."

Marco Prinz, a neuroimmunologist at the University of Freiburg who was not involved in the study, described the discovery as a "milestone finding."

Prinz said what made the finding significant was the unexpected organization of the immune cells.

"I think nobody expected to find these lymph node-like structures in the skull," he told DW.

But Prinz stressed that researchers have yet to demonstrate that the hubs themselves exist and function in humans.

"The major challenge, however, will be to see them in the human skull as well and to show that they are functional there. This would then indeed change how we view the central nervous system's immune response in humans," Prinz said.

How the immune hubs affected brain tumors

After finding that disrupting the skull immune hubs made brain tumors grow faster, the researchers tested whether strengthening the response could help. They stimulated the skull marrow with immune-boosting proteins. The treated animals rejected tumors more effectively and survived longer.

The experiment raises the possibility of one day targeting the skull's bone marrow to influence the brain's immune defenses, without delivering treatment directly into the brain.

Any such treatment in humans remains a distant prospect.

"We first need to confirm their organization and function in humans, understand how they change across different diseases, and determine how to manipulate them without causing harmful inflammation," Kipnis said.

What this could mean for other brain diseases

The potential implications extend beyond cancer.

Prinz said the structures may be especially important in brain tumors and infections, where the protective blood-brain barrier can become leaky. Their importance in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, where changes to that barrier are generally less pronounced, "has to be shown," he said.

Kipnis expects that, if similar functioning structures are found in humans, their role could be much broader.

"If I had to bet, I would bet that these structures play a role in any brain disease that has an immune component to it," he said.



Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

entries.title: Spiraling health costs force Iranians to delay care
entries.summary: A single chemotherapy session in Iran can cost six times the monthly minimum wage. As drug prices soar and medicine is in short supply, doctors say more patients are delaying or abandoning treatment.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

A single chemotherapy session in Iran can cost six times the monthly minimum wage. As drug prices soar and medicine is in short supply, doctors say more patients are delaying or abandoning treatment.

A 70-year-old woman with advanced breast cancer was supposed to undergo chemotherapy every two weeks. Doctors had scheduled six treatment sessions, each costing around 100 million Iranian tomans (about $530 or €450).

Iran's minimum monthly wage for workers covered by the country's labor law is 16.6 million tomans, meaning that just one of her chemotherapy sessions costs roughly six times the monthly minimum wage.

The woman's children asked her doctor to postpone the next round of treatment while they searched for a loan or any other source of financial support, according to colleagues of Hamid Hemmatpour, an Iranian physician based in Austria and a member of the executive board of the Association of Healthcare Professionals for Human Rights-Austria.

Her story is far from unique. Across Iran, rising prices, persistent shortages, disruptions in foreign currency transfers and growing pressure on the health care system are making access to treatment increasingly difficult, according to Hemmatpour and another Iranian physician based in Austria, Hassan Nayeb Hashem.

Drug prices rise sharply in Iran

In one example, an Iranian pharmaceutical company recently announced price increases for 82 products.

The average price of those medicines rose from roughly 180,000 tomans to 390,000 tomans, an increase of around 120%, according to figures published by Tasnim News Agency, which is affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The list shows particularly steep increases for a number of medicines. Donepezil rose by about 543%, clarithromycin by roughly 308%, and amoxicillin by around 115%. The prices for some acetaminophen and diphenhydramine syrups increased by about 135%.

The figures relate to a single manufacturer, but they illustrate the scale of the financial pressure many patients face.

Insulin users are among those hardest hit. Hemmatpour said the cost of a monthly prescription of four NovoRapid insulin pens has risen from about 280,000 tomans after insurance reimbursement to roughly 1.1 million tomans.

When patients delay treatment

Hassan Nayeb Hashem warns that shrinking access to vital treatments could have tragic consequences.

"If the medicine becomes inaccessible, patients can develop complications much sooner," he told DW. "The most serious risk is premature death."

In many cases, switching medications is not a practical solution.

"For many specific diseases, there is effectively no substitute," he added.

Cancer patients are particularly vulnerable because treatment schedules are often tightly structured. Delays can reduce the effectiveness of therapy and affect outcomes.

Hamid Hemmatpour says some patients ask physicians abroad to obtain cancer medicines, while others postpone or abandon treatment after learning the cost.

The cancer drug Keytruda (pembrolizumab) is one example. An Iranian-produced version can cost around 70 million tomans, more than four times the monthly minimum wage, according to Hemmatpour. Imported Indian versions may sell for around 300 million tomans, European versions can cost even more.

Not surprisingly, experts report rising demand for medicines obtained through unofficial cross-border channels.

"The question is under what conditions these medicines were transported," Hemmatpour said. "Some of these drugs require refrigerated transport. Patients often have no way of knowing whether proper storage conditions were maintained during the journey."

Hemmatpour and Nayeb Hashem also warn that imported drugs may be counterfeit or expired, potentially reducing their effectiveness and posing additional health risks.

Why medicine shortages persist in Iran

Many of the country's health challenges predate the current war. Iran's pharmaceutical industry had already been struggling with a weakening currency, rising production costs and delayed payments from insurers.

US sanctions added another layer of difficulty. Medicines and humanitarian goods are generally exempt from sanctions, but restrictions on banking transactions and international payments can complicate pharmaceutical trade. 



Iranian officials have attributed part of the current shortage to a disruption of supply chains and difficulties in transferring foreign currency.

Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of Iran's Food and Drug Administration, has said money transfers slowed dramatically after the war began, nearly coming to a standstill for one to two months and continuing at a reduced pace for several months afterward.

At the same time, Abdolnaser Hemmati, governor of the Central Bank of Iran, says the amount of foreign currency allocated for medicines and medical equipment during the first five months of the current Iranian year was 30% higher than the same period a year earlier.

The statements suggest the problem extends beyond the amount of foreign currency allocated. Delays in payments, imports, manufacturing or distribution can all contribute to shortages.

Why Iran faces a deeper medicine crisis

Medicine shortages are not unique to Iran. In recent years, countries including Germany and the United States have also faced shortages of antibiotics, cancer therapies and other essential medicines, partly because of manufacturing problems and vulnerabilities within global supply chains made especially clear by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Iran's situation is particularly difficult as it finds itself facing the brunt of several pressures at the same time.

Currency depreciation, rising production costs, pressure on insurers, sanctions-related obstacles and the economic consequences of war have all converged on a health care system that was already weak.

Salman Eshaghi, spokesman for the Health and Treatment Committee of Iran's parliament, says around 43 medicines are currently classified as being in "critical shortage," while nearly 1,000 pharmaceutical products face some degree of shortage.

He says higher prices for medicines used to treat cancer, hemophilia and thalassemia have already caused some patients to reduce treatment or stop it altogether.

Originally, patients were expected to pay about 30% of health care costs, with insurers and the government covering the rest, according to Eshaghi. But now patients are paying more than 70% out of pocket.

For the 70-year-old woman with breast cancer, however, the broader debates and international wrangling do not alter her predicament.

Her doctor recommended treatment and her family wanted her to continue, but they simply could not afford the next chemotherapy session. It remains postponed while her children hunt for a way to pay for it.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: India news: Police used 'excessive force' on CJP protesters
entries.summary: Amnesty International alleges that police in the capital New Delhi and the state of Bihar used excessive force against youth-led Cockroach protesters. Full details and more in DW's roundup of major headlines in India.
entries.content:
India

India news: Police used 'excessive force' on CJP protesters

Published August 24, 2026last updated August 24, 2026

Amnesty International alleges that police in the capital New Delhi and the state of Bihar used excessive force against youth-led Cockroach protesters. Full details and more in DW's roundup of major headlines in India.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are our rolling updates from India on Monday, August 24:

  • Amnesty International has released a report saying that police used disproportionate force during India's Gen Z protests
  • Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar is visiting Russia
  • Three babies have died in a hospital fire in Maharashtra

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Foreign Minister Jaishankar meets Russian President Putin, says economic cooperation has grown

Foreign Minister Jaishankar meets Russian President Putin, says economic cooperation has grown

Indian Minister of External Affairs S Jaishankar met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Monday.

Jaishankar told Putin that the economic cooperation between the two countries has grown "very significantly."

"We have a very strong picture of cooperation to present," Jaishankar told the Russian leader after he co-chaired ⁠a meeting ​of ​the India-Russia ​Inter-Governmental ‌Commission on Trade, Economic, ​Scientific, ⁠Technological and Cultural Cooperation on Monday.

The foreign minister conveyed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi looked forward to welcoming Putin at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi which kicks off on September 12. 

Skip next section India National Security Advisor Ajit Doval in China for border talks

India National Security Advisor Ajit Doval in China for border talks

India's National Security Advisor Ajit Doval has arrived in China ahead of talks scheduled for Tuesday on the disputed India-China border in the Himalayas.

Doval — who is India's Special Representative on the India-China Boundary Question — reached Beijing on Monday afternoon on a two-day visit, India's Foreign Ministry said in a press statement.

The Indian top security official's visit comes at the invitation of Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the statement added.

Doval is set to meet Yi on Tuesday for border talks.

"At this meeting, the two sides will, in accordance with the spirit of the consensus reached by the leaders of the two countries, continue to engage in in-depth communication on the boundary question and jointly safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas," news agency AFP quoted Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian as telling the media.

Doval will also meet China's Vice President Han Zheng during his visit, the foreign ministry in New Delhi said.

India-China border dispute

Tensions flared in India's longstanding border contention with China in 2020 when troops from both sides clashed in the Galwan valley, leaving 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers dead.

The skirmish — which was India and China's first deadly military confrontation since 1975 — put relations between the two nuclear-armed Asian giants under strain.

Indian and Chinese officials have regularly held border talks since the clashes.

India and China discuss border ahead of BRICS

The talks come weeks before India hosts the 18th BRICS Summit in September. New Delhi is hoping that Chinese President Xi Jinping will attend the summit but there is yet to be any statement from Beijing. 

If Xi does come to New Delhi for the summit, it would be his first trip to India since the 2020 standoff.

WATCH — Can India's Gen Z turn climate awareness into action?

India's young climate activists want to help those hardest hit by environmental degradation but how can they mobilize the masses?

Find out in this report:



Skip next section Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar in Russia

Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar in Russia

India's Foreign Minister S Jaishankar  is visiting the Russian capital of Moscow for the 27th Session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation, which he is co-chairing.

Jaishankar's two-day trip, which began Sunday, comes at the invitation of Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov, India's Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement last week.

Jaishankar is slated to meet his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov during the visit and exchange views on regional and global issues, the ministry said.

Jaishankar visit comes as New Delhi and Moscow continue to bolster their long-standing relationship, which spans decades and is deeply rooted in history, trade and defense.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, New Delhi has been under pressure from Kyiv's western partners over its cooperation with Moscow. 

Observers say India has adopted a neutral stance on the Ukraine war.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said during talks last year with Russian President Vladimir Putin that India was "not neutral" and had a side, which he elaborated was the "side of peace".

On Monday, Jaishakar sent greetings on X to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Ukraine's Independence Day as Kyiv celebrates its separation from the Soviet Union 35 years ago on August 24, 1991,

"Look forward to further deepening our bilateral partnership," Jaishankar said in the post.



 

Skip next section Fire at Maharashtra government hospital leaves three newborns dead

Fire at Maharashtra government hospital leaves three newborns dead

Three newborn babies died in an early morning fire at a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit of a government hospital in Amravati in India's western Maharashtra on Monday.

The fire broke out around 3.30 a.m. local time at the District Women's Hospital after a ventilator suddenly exploded, Indian media reports said.

The unit where the fire started is meant for premature and critically-ill babies.

Maharashtra Revenue Minister and Amravati District's Guardian Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule said in a statement that the hospital staff safely evacuated the other babies in the unit as soon as the fire erupted.

According to news agencies ANI and PTI, 39 infants were admitted to the unit when the blaze started.

Six babies have been moved to another hospital for treatment, reports cited officials as saying.

The exact cause of the fire is not yet known.

Bawankule said he has ordered a probe into the incident.

Skip next section Amnesty probe singles out use of AK-type assault rifle on Bihar protesters

Amnesty probe singles out use of AK-type assault rifle on Bihar protesters

Amnesty International said that it had verified two videos filmed during the Cockroach movement protests in the eastern state of Bihar's Siwan on July 24, where a police officer is using an AK-type assault rifle against protesters.

"Firearms of this kind are designed to kill and, in the context of assemblies, may lawfully be used only to meet an imminent threat of death or serious injury to a specific individual, and only as an absolute last resort," the organization said, adding that it had found "no evidence any such threat existed."

The Bihar Police told the Supreme Court last Monday that one of their police constables "got trapped in the crowd during the protests and fired four rounds in the air, adding that no one was injured.

The Bihar Police agreed in its account to the court that AK-47 rifle was a "platoon-level weapon" used in special operations and not in crowd control situations.

The Bihar Police. however. maintained that it had not used excessive force.

Skip next section What Delhi Police said about the use of force

What Delhi Police said about the use of force

The Delhi Police has denied the use of excessive force during the July 20 protest march to the Indian parliament that was met with violent police action, triggering allegations of police brutality.

Amnesty's report comes just days after the Supreme Court formed a high-powered enquiry committee to probe the allegations of violence by both police and demonstrators.

Police officials told the Indian top court last week that they used force only after the protests stopped being peaceful.

The Delhi police claimed that anti-social elements "masquerading as aggrieved students" got mixed with the thousands of protesters and caused "grievous injuries" to security forces.

The capital's police told the court that 240 personnel were injured in the clash with protesters.

The Delhi police asserted in the Supreme Court that it used "maximum restraint" while using only the "minimum required force" to control the protest.

Amnesty said that there were "isolated incidents of protesters throwing stones."

Skip next section 'State-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control,' Amnesty alleges

'State-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control,' Amnesty alleges

Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India said in a statement that Indian authorities first "suppressed" the demonstrators right to protest with a communication blackout, barricading and transport disruptions.

"They then attempted to crush it with unnecessary or excessive use of force against peaceful protesters, including children. This heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control. The continued impunity after a month is a testament to that," Patel said.

The protests, which were led by the viral satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), were sparked by the leak of question papers for a highly-competitive national medical college entrance exam. The protests made India's then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan step down. 

The movement is seen as one the biggest challenges for Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his three terms in power. 

The CJP movement has expanded to focus on unemployment and opportunities for young people.

Skip next section Amnesty says police deployed 'unlawful and deadly force' against CJP protesters

Amnesty says police deployed 'unlawful and deadly force' against CJP protesters

Indian police used excessive force — including pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas launchers, grenades, batons and electric shock devices —  in their clampdown of July's youth-driven Cockroach protests, a new digital investigation published by human rights group Amnesty International on Monday alleged. 

Amnesty said that its Evidence Lab had verified video and photographic evidence — along with witness testimony — to confirm the use of the weapons in Delhi and eastern India's Bihar state.

"The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines," Amnesty said in a report that contradicts police claims.

Amnesty says pellet guns used

Amnesty also published an account of an anonymous protester who claimed to have sustained pellet injuries.

"I saw an officer standing roughly 300-400 metres away aiming the (pellet-firing) shotgun towards where I was standing. I started running in the opposite direction and that's when I got hit on my back, otherwise I would have been hit on my face and chest," Amnesty quoted the protester as saying.

The protester told the international human rights organization that doctors had confirmed that they were pellet injuries.

The Delhi police had earlier posted a statement on X deeming reports claiming the use of pellet guns against peaceful protesters as "completely false and misleading".

On Friday, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi reached a Delhi Police station with a 19-year-old protester who said he was wounded by pellets during the July 20 march.

Gandhi staged a sit-in with the protester outside the police station, demanding a police investigation into the shooting. The protester's case was subsequently registered by the police.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi from DW's studio in New Delhi. We are back with our daily digest of all the biggest headlines that are stirring up attention in the world's most populous nation.

The Indian government continues to face criticism in the aftermath of the Cockroach protests, the massive youth-led agitation that rattled Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration as it demanded an overhaul of the country's education system. A new report by Amnesty International says that Indian police used excessive force against protesters in crackdowns on last month's demonstrations.

In a horrifying tragedy, three newborns have died in a fire at a government hospital in the western Indian state of Maharashtra.

And in international relations, India's Foreign Minister S Jaishankar is in Russia, co-chairing the 27th Session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation.

Follow along for all this and more.

entries.title: Germany news: State premier visits VW for crisis talks
entries.summary: Political leaders are visiting car giant Volkswagen for crisis talks, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz meets party colleagues after a testing summer. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: State premier visits VW for crisis talks

Published August 24, 2026last updated August 24, 2026

Political leaders are visiting car giant Volkswagen for crisis talks, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz meets party colleagues after a testing summer. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, August 24, 2026:

  • Lower Saxony's state premier is meeting VW worker representatives, unions and local management
  • The struggling carmaker says it is facing pressure to cut costs while protecting jobs
  • Conservative Christian Democrat leaders are meeting after the summer break
  • The meeting follows tensions over Merz's July reshuffle and upcoming state elections

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section 'Spodyssey' helps drive German cinema comeback

'Spodyssey' helps drive German cinema comeback

Germany's cinemas are enjoying their strongest year since the COVID-19 pandemic, helped by blockbuster releases including "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" and "The Odyssey."

The success of the two very different films has even spawned the nickname "Spodyssey" in English-language media.

Around 47.5 million cinema tickets were sold in Germany in the first half of 2026, according to the German Federal Film Board (FFA).

That was almost 7 million more than in the same period last year, an increase of 16.9%.

Box-office revenue rose even faster, climbing 24.5% to around €502.2 million ($585 million).

Around 6 million fewer tickets were sold than in the first half of 2019, before the pandemic.

Revenue, however, was about 9% higher than in 2019, partly reflecting higher ticket prices.

FFA board member Peter Dinges said the market had reached a level that would have seemed unlikely only a few years ago.

"If the positive development continues, 2026 could become the strongest cinema year since the pandemic," he said.

Skip next section Nearly half of Germans open to humanoid robots at home

Nearly half of Germans open to humanoid robots at home

Almost half of people in Germany could imagine using an AI-powered humanoid robot in their home, according to a new survey.

The Bitkom digital association found 48% were open to the idea, while 47% rejected it.

Among those interested in using one:

  • 87% would have it tidy up.
  • 77% would let it put away shopping.
  • 73% would use it for cleaning.
  • 60% could imagine help with cooking.
  • 58% would use one to care for pets.
  • 55% could imagine help caring for people in need of assistance.
  • 54% would use one for repairs.

"Humanoid robots polarize," Bitkom managing director Bernhard Rohleder said, adding that acceptance would depend on whether they offered practical help in everyday life.

Skip next section German court orders separated couple to auction ownership of dog

German court orders separated couple to auction ownership of dog

A German court has ruled that a separated couple must bid against each other for ownership of their dog after both sought to end the other's co-ownership of the animal.

The Koblenz Regional Court said that because the couple had not been married, rules governing the division of property after divorce did not apply.

Both former partners wanted the other's co-ownership rights to be terminated.

The court rejected an arrangement under which the dog would alternate between them every few weeks because neither wanted to continue sharing ownership.

Since the dog could not literally be divided, the judges said the logical solution was an auction between the two former partners.

The court said the arrangement was also in the animal's interests because the former couple were deeply at odds.

Regular handovers could expose the dog to the severe tensions between them, which the court said would not be compatible with its welfare.

The ruling is not yet final and can be appealed to Germany's Federal Court of Justice.

Skip next section German logistics billionaire Klaus-Michael Kühne dies at 89

German logistics billionaire Klaus-Michael Kühne dies at 89

German logistics billionaire Klaus-Michael Kühne has died at the age of 89.

Business publication Manager Magazin and the newspaper Handelsblatt initially reported on Monday that Kühne had died overnight.

The Kühne Holding group later confirmed the news.

Born in Hamburg in 1937, Kühne joined the family logistics business Kühne+Nagel in 1958 and became its CEO in 1966. The company was co-founded by his grandfather August Kühne in 1890.

Kühne later moved to Switzerland and remained one of the most influential figures in German business.

He was still a member of Kühne+Nagel's board and served as its honorary chairman.

Through Kühne Holding, he built up stakes in several major companies.

He controlled 53% of Kühne+Nagel and 30% of shipping group Hapag-Lloyd. He had also become Lufthansa's largest individual shareholder, with his holding company owning a little over 20% of the airline.

Kühne also provided financial support to his favorite football club, Hamburger SV.

In recent years, Kühne also expanded his investments into companies including chemicals distributor Brenntag and transport operator Flix.

Handelsblatt estimated Kühne's fortune at around €36 billion ($42 billion), making him Germany's second-richest person behind Lidl and Kaufland retail billionaire Dieter Schwarz.

Skip next section German students injured in Netherlands bus crash

German students injured in Netherlands bus crash

Eight people have been injured, some seriously, after a coach carrying mostly German schoolchildren crashed in the Netherlands.

The Austrian-registered bus collided with a van early in the morning on the A28 near Wezep, around 100 kilometers (62 miles) northeast of Amsterdam.

Police said the coach hit the van before smashing through the central barrier and coming to rest on the opposite carriageway.

Eight people were taken to hospital, including the driver of the van. Some of those injured were reported to be in serious condition.

The crash caused extensive damage and the motorway was closed.

Around 50 people were traveling on the coach.

Skip next section Poll shows how worried Germans are after explosive drone found at airport

Poll shows how worried Germans are after explosive drone found at airport

Most Germans are concerned by the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport, according to a new YouGov poll.

The survey found 63% were worried by the incident, while 22% said they were only slightly concerned and 9% said they were not concerned at all.

The drone was discovered on August 4 in a secure area of Leipzig/Halle Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo aircraft.

Authorities have suspected possible Russian involvement, but the origin of the drone has not been established.

The poll also found wider doubts about Germany's ability to protect airports and other critical infrastructure from hostile drones.

  • 50% said Germany was "rather poorly" prepared.
  • 30% said it was "very poorly" prepared.
  • Just 11% considered Germany well prepared.
  • 9% said they did not know.

Supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) were the least concerned, according to the poll.

Only slightly more than a third of AfD voters said the incident worried them.

Among supporters of the populist left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), fewer than half expressed concern.

Skip next section Merz's conservative CDU party leadership meets after summer break

Merz's conservative CDU party leadership meets after summer break

The leadership of Germany's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the ruling center-right party led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is meeting Monday for its first regular talks since the summer break.

The gathering comes after senior party figures sharply criticized personnel decisions made by Merz before the recess in July.

After parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn resigned, Merz initiated eight personnel changes across the government, party leadership and parliamentary group.

Particular anger within the CDU focused on the way Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder was replaced.

Monday's meeting will offer an indication of whether those tensions have eased over the summer.

The party leadership could also discuss a Cabinet retreat scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday as well as state elections due in September, in which the far-right Alternative for Germany is polling especially strongly in eastern states such as Saxony-Anhalt.

No press conference is planned after the meeting.

A YouGov poll published over the weekend found that 54% of Germans expect Merz to leave office before the next scheduled federal election in 2029.

Skip next section State government visits VW plant amid jobs fears

State government visits VW plant amid jobs fears

Lower Saxony state premier Olaf Lies is due to visit Volkswagen's Hanover plant for talks on the future of the struggling carmaker.

Lies, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party, was invited by Volkswagen's general works council and is expected to meet employee representatives, staff delegates and local plant management.

The talks are expected to focus on Volkswagen's restructuring plans and the future of its German production sites.

Afterward, Lies is due to brief the media alongside Lower Saxony deputy state premier Julia Willie Hamburg of the Green Party, works council chief Daniela Cavallo and representatives of the IG Metall trade union.

The state of Lower Saxony holds a 20% ownership stake in the Volkswagen Group.

Lies is also planning visits to VW plants in Osnabrück and Emden, while talks with representatives of the Zwickau factory in the eastern state of Saxony are expected to take place online.

Volkswagen is trying to cut costs and improve competitiveness, raising concerns over jobs and the future of several plants.

Workers, unions and politicians are seeking assurances over tens of thousands of jobs.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies is set to visit Volkswagen's Hanover plant for talks on the future of the struggling carmaker.

He was invited by VW’s general works council. VW is trying to cut costs and improve competitiveness, but workers, unions and politicians are seeking assurances over tens of thousands of jobs.

Meanwhile, the leadership of Germany’s center-right Christian Democratic Union is meeting for its first regular talks since the summer break.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Ukraine news: UK PM Burnham arrives in Kyiv to show support
entries.summary: Andy Burnham's first trip abroad as PM will see him co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing and meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The visit comes as Ukraine marks its 35th independence day. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine news: UK PM Burnham arrives in Kyiv to show support

Published August 24, 2026last updated August 24, 2026

Andy Burnham's first trip abroad as PM will see him co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing and meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The visit comes as Ukraine marks its 35th independence day. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Andy Burnham visits Kyiv on his first overseas trip since becoming the UK's prime minister
  • Burnham is set to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing and meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
  • Ukraine has been calling for its allies to supply more air defenses and apply more pressure on Russia, which has escalated its attacks on civilians in recent weeks
  • The meeting coincides with the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence from the Soviet Union
  • Ukraine hits facilities belonging to Russia's second-biggest e-commerce website Ozon
  • The United Nations Security Council is scheduled to hold a special session on Ukraine later on Monday

Here is a roundup of the main developments related to Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, August 24, 2026:

Skip next section UK's Burnham hails Ukraine as 'Europe's protector'

UK's Burnham hails Ukraine as 'Europe's protector'

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Ukraine was "Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."

Speaking in Kyiv alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Council President Antonio Costa, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight against Nazi Germany.

"My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st."

Burnham, making his first visit to the Ukrainian capital as prime minister, was due to announce British support to help Kyiv boost its domestic production of long-range missiles, a move the Kremlin has criticized while also warning the UK of "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv.

"Despite Russia's outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine's defence," Burnham said.

Skip next section Costa says Ukraine's EU future is key to long-term security

Costa says Ukraine's EU future is key to long-term security

President of the European Council Antonio Costa has said the European Union will continue supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary, "during the war, in future peace negotiations and in reconstruction."

Speaking in Kyiv at a ceremony marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence, Costa has said Ukraine's future in the European Union is the strongest guarantee of long-term security and democratic stability.

He has said Ukraine's accession process will be challenging but should not be blocked by political hesitation.

Costa has said Russia has failed to achieve its objectives after more than four years of full-scale war, despite the heavy human and economic costs.

Costa has added the EU wants to see a peaceful resolution of the conflict.

"We support all serious initiatives aimed at achieving peace in Ukraine. But ultimately, it is Ukraine - and only Ukraine - that must define the terms of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace," he said.

"That peace must affirm Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. And it must guarantee Ukraine's long-term security and its ability to defend itself," Costa added.

Skip next section Kremlin says UK 'preventing peace' in Ukraine

Kremlin says UK 'preventing peace' in Ukraine

Russia accused the UK of being a participant in the war on Ukraine's side.

The accusation comes as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham reportedly plans to provide Ukraine with plans to build its own SCALP long-range cruise missiles, capable of hitting targets deep into Russia.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to ​the fire and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow.

He added Russia would target and "destroy" facilities producing the missiles in Ukraine.

Skip next section Ukraine wants peace but won't surrender, Zelenskyy says

Ukraine wants peace but won't surrender, Zelenskyy says

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his country wants peace, but will not surrender territory to Russia to end the war.

"Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it's not ready to simply surrender," Zelenskyy said.

Speaking during Ukraine's Independence Day celebrations, Zelenskyy rejected Russian demands that Ukraine give up the remaining parts of the Donbas region under its control.

"We will not let them [Russians] seize the initiative, deceive Europe ‌and ​the entire world into thinking that we simply need to give up Donbas and everything will be over soon," he said.

Paying tribute to the ​people and soldiers defending Ukraine, Zelenskyy also urged allies to give it "everything" needed to stop the war.

Skip next section Russian military launches Soyuz rocket with spacecraft

Russian military launches Soyuz rocket with spacecraft

Russia launched a Soyuz rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the country's north on Monday, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.

In a statement, the ministry said the rocket was carrying a spacecraft "in the interests of the Russian Ministry of Defense."

The cosmodrome is known for launches that place low-Earth-orbit Rassvet satellites into space, although it was not immediately clear whether this mission was intended for that purpose.

Rassvet is Russia's alternative to SpaceX's Starlink satellite network.

Earlier this month, Ukrainian intelligence officials said Russia plans to have 300 of these satellites in orbit by 2027.

Major General Vadym Skibitsky told RBC-Ukraine: "They have already begun launching it much faster than originally planned."

SpaceX currently has more than 10,000 satellites in orbit. Starlink is banned in Russia, and the use of its equipment can result in fines.

Ukrainian forces use Starlink to communicate on the battlefield.

Skip next section EU approves further €6.1 billion for Ukraine's defense

EU approves further €6.1 billion for Ukraine's defense

The European Commission has approved an additional  €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in financial aid for Ukraine to procure new defense systems.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the money is for "air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs."

The EU said the latest aid package is in addition to €16 billion in previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion has already been disbursed.

Von der Leyen said Europe would stand with Ukraine, "as long as it takes."

Skip next section Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day

Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa have arrived in Kyiv.

Burnham is on his first international visit since becoming prime minister.

He was welcomed by Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, at the train station.

Burnham and Costa will meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later and attend Ukraine's Independence Day celebrations.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldova's President Maia Sandu and Estonia's President Alar Karis, along with Sybiha, were also in the Kyiv to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence.

Skip next section Russia says it hit fuel tanker near Odesa

Russia says it hit fuel tanker near Odesa

Russia's Defence Ministry has said its forces struck a tanker carrying fuel and lubricants for Ukrainian troops at the port of Pivdennyi near the southern city of Odesa.

The ministry said the attack also hit port infrastructure used to unload and store military cargo.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the Russian claims.

Skip next section Ukraine stepping up attacks on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon

Ukraine stepping up attacks on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon

Ukraine has struck warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon on three consecutive days, with the company reporting another logistics center on fire.

The attacks mark an expansion of Kyiv's campaign against Russian logistics infrastructure after weeks of strikes on Wildberries, the country's largest online retailer.

Kyiv has accused Wildberries of supplying components to the Russian military.

Ozon said a "major fire" broke out at one of its logistics centers in the southern Krasnodar region following a drone attack.

"All systems operated as designed, and we promptly evacuated staff. Preliminarily, there are no casualties," the company said on Telegram.

On Sunday, Ozon said a drone attack caused a fire at its logistics hub in the central Orenburg region, forcing the warehouse to suspend operations.

That came a day after another Ozon center was hit in neighboring Samara, where the company said an unspecified number of employees were wounded.

Skip next section WATCH — Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia?

WATCH — Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia?

Russia has a growing manpower problem in its war against Ukraine. Rumors are spreading, and recent border queues near Georgia are drawing comparisons to the chaos of 2022.

Is Russia quietly preparing another draft? DW's Shannon Redstall explains.

Skip next section Why is Ukraine struggling to defend itself against Russian air attacks?

Why is Ukraine struggling to defend itself against Russian air attacks?

In recent weeks and months, Russia has intensified its airstrikes on Ukraine, regularly firing dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, often at civilian targets.

To defend itself, Ukraine relies on advanced, foreign-made weapons systems — most importantly, US Patriot missiles.

The US war with Iran has depleted its own stockpiles, and Washington has resisted providing Kyiv with large numbers of missiles, leaving Ukraine more exposed to Russian bombs.

Even before the war with Iran, US support for Ukraine had wavered after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump, who had an angry public spat with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House, has sought to mend ties with Russia's Vladimir Putin, and ordered a pause of US military aid to Kyiv.

Over the weekend, Zelenskyy revealed that deliveries of Patriot interceptors had dropped by 50% since 2023.

"Over the entire year of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 — 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," he said. "For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264."

Skip next section Debris from Ukrainian drone kills two children in southern Russia: governor

Debris from Ukrainian drone kills two children in southern Russia: governor

Falling debris from a Ukrainian drone attack landed on a childcare facility in Krasnodar, southern Russia, killing two children, the regional governor said early on Monday.

Seven other children and two adults were wounded in the attack, Veniamin Kondratyev said on Telegram. He added that a fire started at a warehouse after a drone fell on it.

Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, said there was a "major fire" at one of its logistics centers in Krasnodar as a result of a drone attack.

Another Ozon logistics complex in Dagestan was also hit, sparking a massive fire, Ukrainian monitor Exilenova+ reported. If confirmed, it would be the third Ozon facility to be struck on Monday.

Ukraine has also hit warehouses belonging to Russia's other major e-commerce website, Wildberries, in recent weeks.

While Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure, it has also struck commercial hubs and warehouses, which are easier targets and less heavily defended than military or energy sites. The attacks have inflicted losses worth billions of dollars.

Skip next section Russian strike on Kharkiv kills 3

Russian strike on Kharkiv kills 3

At least three people were killed after a Russian attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv, the local governor said on Telegram.

Oleh Syniehuhov said eight people were rescued by the emergency services, which were still working to identify other potential casualties.

Kharkiv is Ukraine's second-largest city, and lies around 30 kilometers (about 18 miles) from the border with Russia.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?

IN DEPTH: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?

Empty pumps, long waits: Attacks on oil refineries have left Russia increasingly short of fuel. Dissident Russian economists say growing anger about shortages among ordinary Russians could help end the war in Ukraine.

Learn more about how Ukraine's drone strikes inside Russia are triggering a fuel crisis that could bring about the end of the war in this report.

Skip next section Ex-Ukrainian minister didn't call for elections until dismissed from government, lawmaker tells DW

Ex-Ukrainian minister didn't call for elections until dismissed from government, lawmaker tells DW

Dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for elections earlier this week, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy comes under unprecedented pressure domestically.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion began more than four years ago. Zelenskyy has resisted holding elections while the country remains at war with Russia.

Ukrainian Member of Parliament Yevheniia Kravchuk spoke to DW from Kyiv about the prospect of Ukraine holding elections while still fighting the Russian invasion. 

Here's what Kravchuk had to say about Fedorov's appeal for elections:

"You know, Mykhailo wasn't speaking about elections when he was in the government for seven years, almost seven years. So, the first time he started to speak about it was when he basically lost his position in the government during the reshuffle."

On the prospect of a wartime poll, she said:

"War is not a normal situation for people, for elections — it's not normal to live. But we have to; it's been almost five years.

Martial law does put restrictions, and these restrictions are there for a reason. And it is because Russians are throwing missiles at supermarkets."

Watch this video for more of Yevheniia Kravchuk's interview with DW News, as well as insight from Harry Nedelcu, a geopolitics expert at Rasmussen Global consultancy in Brussels:

entries.title: New Zealand proposes social media ban for under-16s
entries.summary: The government is set to follow Australia's lead and introduce a bill banning children from social media. But the plan already faces opposition from within the ruling coalition.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

The government is set to follow Australia's lead and introduce a bill banning children from social media. But the plan already faces opposition from within the ruling coalition.

New Zealand's government is set to introduce legislation Monday banning children under the age of 16 from social media, following the lead of several countries across the world, including neighbor Australia. 

What does New Zealand's social media ban entail?

The Online Safety Bill would require platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook to verify users are 16 or older using tools such as facial age estimation and digital ID, with fines of up to 10% of global revenue for non-compliance.

​​Platforms would also have to assess the risks they pose to young users and report on efforts to reduce them.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the harm to children is too great to ignore.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," he said, citing effects on mental health, sleep and education. The government's data shows one in three children aged 13 to 17 now spend at least five hours a day on social media.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the bill places the legal burden on platforms, not families: "No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers."

Will the bill really be introduced?

Even though New Zealand spent more than a year examining the potential ban, the bill's future is uncertain, as coalition partners NZ First and ACT have both voiced opposition, questioning the law's effectiveness. 

 Australia's similar ban took effect last year, barring under-16s from platforms including Facebook, Instagram and TikTok as part of an effort to shield children from bullying and "predatory algorithms." But a June peer-reviewed study by Australian researchers found little evidence it reduced teen social media use.

Edited by: Rob Turner
